entries.ae4dcd4f28f96daff976764e4e022ccbe8a22470: <div sID="gen18322" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Lam.4" sID="Lam.4"/> <div eID="gen18322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18323" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18324" type="x-p"/> This chapter is another single alphabet of Lamentations for the destruction of Jerusalem, like those in the first two chapters. I. The prophet here laments the injuries and indignities done to those to whom respect used to be shown, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He laments the direful effects of the famine to which they were reduced by the siege, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3-Lam.4.10">ver. 3-10</reference>. III. He laments the taking and sacking of Jerusalem and its amazing desolations, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.11-Lam.4.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. IV. He acknowledges that the sins of their leaders were the cause of all these calamities, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.13-Lam.4.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. V. He gives up all as doomed to utter ruin, for their enemies were every way too hard for them, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.17-Lam.4.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. VI. He foretels the destruction of the Edomites who triumphed in Jerusalem's fall, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">ver. 21</reference>. VII. He foretels the return of the captivity of Zion at last, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">ver. 22</reference>.
entries.9d745a8868fc4c10d09371afa90b9e8581cf7b4e: <div eID="gen18324" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18323" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Desolate Condition of Jerusalem; Effects of Famine in Jerusalem; Destruction of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  588.)</title> <div sID="gen18325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> How is the gold become dim! <hi type="italic">how</hi> is the most fine gold changed! the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street. <hi type="super">2</hi> The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter! <hi type="super">3</hi> Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people <hi type="italic">is become</hi> cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. <hi type="super">4</hi> The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, <hi type="italic">and</hi> no man breaketh <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto them. <hi type="super">5</hi> They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills. <hi type="super">6</hi> For the punishment of the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the punishment of the sin of Sodom, that was overthrown as in a moment, and no hands stayed on her. <hi type="super">7</hi> Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing <hi type="italic">was</hi> of sapphire: <hi type="super">8</hi> Their visage is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets: their skin cleaveth to their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">They that be</hi> slain with the sword are better than <hi type="italic">they that be</hi> slain with hunger: for these pine away, stricken through for <hi type="italic">want of</hi> the fruits of the field. <hi type="super">10</hi> The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children: they were their meat in the destruction of the daughter of my people. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath accomplished his fury; he hath poured out his fierce anger, and hath kindled a fire in Zion, and it hath devoured the foundations thereof. <hi type="super">12</hi> The kings of the earth, and all the inhabitants of the world, would not have believed that the adversary and the enemy should have entered into the gates of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen18325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> The elegy in this chapter begins with a lamentation of the very sad and doleful change which the judgments of God had made in Jerusalem. The city that was formerly <hi type="italic">as gold,</hi> as <hi type="italic">the most fine gold,</hi> so rich and splendid, <hi type="italic">the perfection of beauty and the joy of the whole earth,</hi> has become dim, and is changed, has lost its lustre, lost its value, is not what it was; it has become dross. Alas! what an alteration is here! <div eID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> I. The temple was laid waste, which was the glory of Jerusalem and its protection. It is given up into the hands of the enemy. And some understand the gold spoken of (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">v. 1</reference>) to be the <hi type="italic">gold of the temple,</hi> the fine gold with which it was overlaid (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.22">1 Kings vi. 22</reference>); when the temple was burned the gold of it was smoked and sullied, as if it had been of little value. It was thrown among the rubbish; it <hi type="italic">was changed,</hi> converted to common uses and made nothing of. <hi type="italic">The stones of the sanctuary,</hi> which were curiously wrought, were thrown down by the Chaldeans, when they demolished it, or were brought down by the force of the fire, and were <hi type="italic">poured out,</hi> and thrown about <hi type="italic">in the top of every street;</hi> they lay mingled without distinction among the common ruins. When the God of the sanctuary was by sin provoked to withdraw no wonder that the stones of the sanctuary were thus profaned. <div eID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> II. The princes and priests, who were in a special manner the <hi type="italic">sons of Zion,</hi> were trampled upon and abused, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">v. 2</reference>. Both the house of God and the house of David were in Zion. The sons of both those houses were upon this account precious, that they were heirs to the privileges of those two covenants of priesthood and royalty. They were <hi type="italic">comparable to fine gold.</hi> Israel was more rich in them than in treasures of gold and silver. But now they are <hi type="italic">esteemed as earthen pitchers;</hi> they are broken as <hi type="italic">earthen pitchers,</hi> thrown by as vessels in which there is no pleasure. They have grown poor, and are brought into captivity, and thereby are rendered mean and despicable, and every one treads upon them and insults over them. Note, The contempt put upon God's people ought to be matter of lamentation to us. <div eID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> III. Little children were starved for want of bread and water, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3-Lam.4.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The nursing-mothers, having no meat for themselves, had no milk for the babes at their breast, so that, though in disposition they were really compassionate, yet in fact they seemed to be cruel, <hi type="italic">like the ostriches in the wilderness, that leave their eggs in the dust</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.39.14-Job.39.15">Job xxxix. 14, 15</reference>); having no food for their children, they were forced to neglect them and do what they could to forget them, because it was a pain to them to think of them when they had nothing for them; in this they were worse than the seals, or <hi type="italic">sea-monsters,</hi> or <hi type="italic">whales</hi> (as some render it), for they <hi type="italic">drew out the breast, and gave suck to their young,</hi> which <hi type="italic">the daughter of my people</hi> will not do. Children cannot shift for themselves as grown people can; and therefore it was the more painful to see <hi type="italic">the tongue of the sucking-child cleave to the roof of his mouth for thirst,</hi> because there was not a drop of water to moisten it; and to hear the young children, that could but just speak, <hi type="italic">ask bread</hi> of their parents, who had none to give them, no, nor any friend that could supply them. As doleful as our thoughts are of this case, so thankful should our thoughts be of the great plenty we enjoy, and the food convenient we have for ourselves and for our children, and for <hi type="italic">those of our own house.</hi> <div eID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18330" type="x-p"/> IV. Persons of good rank were reduced to extreme poverty, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.5">v. 5</reference>. Those who were well-born and well bred, and had been accustomed to the best, both for food and clothing, who had <hi type="italic">fed delicately,</hi> had every thing that was curious and nice (they call it <hi type="italic">eating well,</hi> whereas those only eat well who eat to the glory of God), and <hi type="italic">fared sumptuously every day;</hi> they had not only been <hi type="italic">advanced to the scarlet,</hi> but from their beginning were <hi type="italic">brought up in scarlet,</hi> and were never acquainted with any thing mean or ordinary. They were <hi type="italic">brought up upon scarlet</hi> (so the word is); their foot-cloths, and the carpets they walked on, were scarlet, yet these, being stripped of all by the war, are <hi type="italic">desolate in the streets,</hi> have not a house to put their head in, nor a bed to lie on, nor clothes to cover them, nor fire to warm them. They <hi type="italic">embrace dunghills;</hi> on them they were glad to lie to get a little rest, and perhaps raked in the dunghills for something to eat, as the prodigal son who <hi type="italic">would fain have filled his belly with the husks.</hi> Note, Those who live in the greatest pomp and plenty know not what straits they may be reduced to before they die; as sometimes the <hi type="italic">needy</hi> are <hi type="italic">raised out of the dunghill. Those who were full have hired out themselves for bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1 Sam. ii. 5</reference>. It is therefore the wisdom of those who have abundance not to use themselves too nicely, for then hardships, when they come, will be doubly hard, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deut. xxviii. 56</reference>. <div eID="gen18330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18331" type="x-p"/> V. Persons who were eminent for dignity, nay, perhaps for sanctity, shared with others in the common calamity, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.7-Lam.4.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Her Nazarites</hi> are extremely charged. Some understand it only of her honourable ones, the young gentlemen, who were very clean, and neat, and well-dressed, washed and perfumed; but I see not why we may not understand it of those devout people among them who <hi type="italic">separated themselves to the Lord</hi> by the <hi type="italic">Nazarites'</hi> vow, <reference osisRef="Num.6.2">Num. vi. 2</reference>. That there were such among them in the most degenerate times appears from <reference osisRef="Amos.2.11">Amos ii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">I raised up of your young men for Nazarites.</hi> These <hi type="italic">Nazarites,</hi> though they were not to cut their hair, yet by reason of their temperate diet, their frequent washings, and especially the pleasure they had in devoting themselves to God and conversing with him, which made their faces to shine as <hi type="italic">Moses's,</hi> were <hi type="italic">purer than snow</hi> and <hi type="italic">whiter than milk;</hi> drinking no wine nor strong drink, they had a more healthful complexion and cheerful countenance than those who regaled themselves daily with the blood of the grape, as <hi type="italic">Daniel</hi> and his fellows with <hi type="italic">pulse and water.</hi> Or it may denote the great respect and veneration which all good people had for them; though perhaps to the eye they had <hi type="italic">no form nor comeliness,</hi> yet, being separated to the Lord, they were valued as if they had been <hi type="italic">more ruddy than rubies and their polishing had been of sapphire.</hi> But now <hi type="italic">their visage is marred</hi> (as is said of Christ, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Isa. lii. 14</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">blacker than a coal;</hi> they look miserably, partly through hunger and partly through grief and perplexity. <hi type="italic">They are not known in the streets;</hi> those who respected them now take no notice of them, and those who had been intimately acquainted with them now scarcely knew them, their countenance was so altered by the miseries that attended the long siege. <hi type="italic">Their skin cleaves to their bones,</hi> their flesh being quite consumed and wasted away; it is <hi type="italic">withered;</hi> it has <hi type="italic">become like a stick,</hi> as dry and hard as a piece of wood. Note, It is a thing to be much lamented that even those who are separated to God are yet, when desolating judgments are abroad, often involved with others in the common calamity. <div eID="gen18331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18332" type="x-p"/> VI. Jerusalem came down slowly, and died a lingering death; for the famine contributed more to her destruction than any other judgment whatsoever. Upon this account the destruction of <hi type="italic">Jerusalem was greater than that of Sodom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">v. 6</reference>), for that was <hi type="italic">overthrown in a moment;</hi> one shower of fire and brimstone dispatched it; <hi type="italic">no hand staid on her;</hi> she did not endure any long siege, as Jerusalem has done; she fell immediately into the <hi type="italic">hands of the Lord,</hi> who strikes home at a blow, and did not <hi type="italic">fall into the hands of man,</hi> who, being weak, is long in doing execution, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.21">Judg. viii. 21</reference>. Jerusalem is kept many months upon the rack, in pain and misery, and dies by inches, dies so as to feel herself die. And, when the iniquity of Jerusalem is more aggravated than that of Sodom, no wonder that the punishment of it is so. Sodom never had the means of grace the Jerusalem had, the oracles of God and his prophets, and therefore the condemnation of Jerusalem will be <hi type="italic">more intolerable</hi> than that of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.23-Matt.11.24">Matt. xi. 23, 24</reference>. The extremity of the famine is here set forth by two frightful instances of it:—1. The tedious deaths that it was the cause of (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.9">v. 9</reference>); many were slain with hunger, were famished to death, their stores being spent, and the public stores so nearly spent that they could not have any relief out of them. They were <hi type="italic">stricken through, for want of the fruits of the field;</hi> those who were starved were as sure to die as if they had been stabbed and stricken through; only their case was much more miserable. <hi type="italic">Those who are slain with the sword</hi> are soon put out of their pain; <hi type="italic">in a moment they go down to the grave,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.13">Job xxi. 13</reference>. They have not the terror of seeing death make its advances towards them, and scarcely feel it when the blow is given; it is but one sharp struggle, and the work is done. And, if we be ready for another world, we need not be afraid of a short passage to it; the quicker the better. But those who die by famine pine away; hunger preys upon their spirits and wastes them gradually; nay, and it frets their spirits, and fills them with vexation, and is as great a torture to the mind as to the body. There are <hi type="italic">bands in their death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.4">Ps. lxxiii. 4</reference>. 2. The barbarous murders that it was the occasion of (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The hands of the pitiful women have</hi> first slain and then <hi type="italic">sodden their own children.</hi> This was lamented before (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">ch. ii. 20</reference>); and it was a thing to be greatly lamented that any should be so wicked as to do it and that they should be brought to such extremities as to be tempted to it. But this horrid effect of long sieges had been threatened in general (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev. xxvi. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deut. xxviii. 53</reference>), and particularly against Jerusalem in the siege of the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jer. xix. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Ezek. v. 10</reference>. The case was sad enough that they had not wherewithal to feed their children and make meat for them (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.4">v. 4</reference>), but much worse that they could find in their hearts to feed upon their children and make meat of them. I know not whether to make it an instance of the power of necessity or of the power of iniquity; but, as the Gentile idolaters were justly <hi type="italic">given up to vile affections</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.26">Rom. i. 26</reference>), so these Jewish idolaters, and the women particularly, who had <hi type="italic">made cakes to the queen of heaven</hi> and taught their children to do so too, were <hi type="italic">stripped of natural affection</hi> and that to their own children. Being thus left to <hi type="italic">dishonour their own nature</hi> was a righteous judgment upon them for the dishonour they had done to God. <div eID="gen18332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18333" type="x-p"/> VII. Jerusalem comes down utterly and wonderfully. 1. The destruction of Jerusalem is a complete destruction (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has accomplished his fury;</hi> he has made thorough work of it, has executed all that he purposed in wrath against Jerusalem, and has remitted no part of the sentence. He has poured out the full vials of his fierce anger, poured them out to the bottom, even the dregs of them. He has <hi type="italic">kindled a fire in Zion,</hi> which has not only consumed the houses, and levelled them with the ground, but, beyond what other fires do, has <hi type="italic">devoured the foundations thereof,</hi> as if they were to be no more built upon. 2. It is an amazing destruction, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.12">v. 12</reference>. It was a surprise to the kings of the earth, who are acquainted with, and inquisitive about, the state of their neighbours; nay, it was so to <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants of the world</hi> who knew Jerusalem, or had ever heard or read of it; they <hi type="italic">could not have believed that the adversary and enemy would ever enter into the gates of Jerusalem;</hi> for, (1.) They knew that Jerusalem was strongly fortified, not only by walls and bulwarks, but by the numbers and strength of its inhabitants; the strong hold of Zion was thought to be impregnable. (2.) They knew that it was the <hi type="italic">city of the great King,</hi> where the Lord of the whole earth had in a more peculiar manner his residence; it was the holy city, and therefore they thought that it was so much under the divine protection that it would be in vain for any of its enemies to make an attack upon it. (3.) They knew that many an attempt made upon it had been baffled, witness that of Sennacherib. They were therefore amazed when they heard of the Chaldeans making themselves masters of it, and concluded that it was certainly by an immediate hand of God that Jerusalem was given up to them; it was by a commission from him that the enemy broke through and entered the gates of Jerusalem.
entries.5e3db72a898ef81a07ab6eecc993dcf9b79d7bbd: <div eID="gen18333" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cause of Jerusalem's Sorrows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18334" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> For the sins of her prophets, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her, <hi type="super">14</hi> They have wandered <hi type="italic">as</hi> blind <hi type="italic">men</hi> in the streets, they have polluted themselves with blood, so that men could not touch their garments. <hi type="super">15</hi> They cried unto them, Depart ye; <hi type="italic">it is</hi> unclean; depart, depart, touch not: when they fled away and wandered, they said among the heathen, They shall no more sojourn <hi type="italic">there.</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> The anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath divided them; he will no more regard them: they respected not the persons of the priests, they favoured not the elders. <hi type="super">17</hi> As for us, our eyes as yet failed for our vain help: in our watching we have watched for a nation <hi type="italic">that</hi> could not save <hi type="italic">us.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> They hunt our steps, that we cannot go in our streets: our end is near, our days are fulfilled; for our end is come. <hi type="super">19</hi> Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven: they pursued us upon the mountains, they laid wait for us in the wilderness. <hi type="super">20</hi> The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , was taken in their pits, of whom we said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen. <div eID="gen18334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18335" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen18335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18336" type="x-p"/> I. The sins they were charged with, for which God brought this destruction upon them, and which served to justify God in it (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.13-Lam.4.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): It is <hi type="italic">for the sins of her prophets,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">iniquities of her priests.</hi> Not that the people were innocent; no, they <hi type="italic">loved to have it so</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jer. v. 31</reference>), and it was to please them that the prophets and priests did as they did; but the fault is chiefly laid upon them, who should have taught them better, should have reproved and admonished them, and told them what would be in the end hereof; of the hands of those watchmen who did not give them warning will their blood be required. Note, Nothing ripens a people more for ruin, nor fills the measure faster, than the sins of their priests and prophets. The particular sin charged upon them is persecution; the false prophets and corrupt priests joined their power and interest to <hi type="italic">shed the blood of the just in the midst of her,</hi> the blood of God's prophets and of those that adhered to them. They not only shed the blood of their innocent children, whom they sacrificed to Moloch, but the blood of the righteous men that were among them, whom they sacrificed to that more cruel idol of enmity to the truth and true religion. This was that sin which the Lord would not pardon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>) and which brought the last destruction upon Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.6">Jam. v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have condemned and killed the just.</hi> And the priests and prophets were the ringleaders in persecution, as in Christ's time the chief priests and scribes were the men that incensed the people against him, who otherwise would have persisted in their hosannas. Now these are those that <hi type="italic">wandered as blind men in the streets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.14">v. 14</reference>. They strayed from the paths of justice, were blind to every thing that is good, but to do evil they were quick-sighted. God says of corrupt judges, <hi type="italic">They know not, neither do they understand; they walk in darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>); and Christ says of the corrupt teachers, <hi type="italic">They are blind leaders of the blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.14">Matt. xv. 14</reference>. They have so <hi type="italic">polluted themselves with</hi> innocent <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> the blood of the saints, that <hi type="italic">men could not touch their garments;</hi> they made themselves odious to all about them, so that good men were as shy of touching them as of touching a dead body, which contracted a ceremonial pollution, or of touching the bloody clothes of one slain, which tender spirits care not to do. There is nothing that will make prophets and priests to be abhorred so much as a spirit of persecution. <div eID="gen18336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18337" type="x-p"/> II. The testimony of their neighbours produced in evidence against them, both to convict them of sin and to show the equity of God's proceedings against them. Some that have grown very impudent in sin boast that they <hi type="italic">care not what people say of them;</hi> but God, by the prophet, would have the Jews to take notice of what people said of them and what was the opinion of the standers by concerning them (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.15-Lam.4.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), what they said, nay, what <hi type="italic">they cried unto them,</hi> especially to the corrupt priests and prophets, <hi type="italic">among the heathen.</hi> 1. They upbraided them with their pretended purity, while they lived in all manner of real iniquity. They cried to them, "<hi type="italic">Depart you; it is unclean.</hi> You were so precise that you would not touch a Gentile, by cried, <hi type="italic">Depart, depart; stand by thyself; I am holier than thou,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. Thus the prosecutors of Christ would not go <hi type="italic">into the judgment-hall, lest they should be defiled.</hi> "But can you now keep the Gentiles from touching you, when God has delivered you into their hands? When you flee away and wander you will bid them stand off and not touch you, because they are unclean. But in vain; these serpents will not be charmed or enchanted thus; no, they will not <hi type="italic">respect the persons of the priests,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">favour the elders;</hi> the most venerable persons will to them be despicable." 2. They upbraided them with their sins, and the anger of God against them for their sins, and the direful effects of that anger. <hi type="italic">They cried to them, Depart you; it is unclean.</hi> They all cried out shame on them, and could easily foresee that God would not long suffer so provoking a people to continue in so good a land. They knew their <hi type="italic">statutes and judgments were righteous,</hi> and expected they should be <hi type="italic">a wise and understanding people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deut. iv. 6</reference>. But, when they saw them quite otherwise, they cried, <hi type="italic">Depart, depart;</hi> they soon read their doom, that the land would spue them out, as it had done their predecessors, and, when they saw the dispersed of <hi type="italic">Jacob fleeing and wandering,</hi> they told them of it. They said, Now <hi type="italic">the anger of the Lord has divided them,</hi> has dispersed them into all countries, because <hi type="italic">they respected not the persons of the priests,</hi> the pious priests that were among them, such as Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, Jeremiah, and others; neither did they <hi type="italic">favour the elders,</hi> but despised them and their authority when they went about to check them for their vicious courses. The very heathen foresaw that this would ruin them. 3. They triumphed in their ruin as irrecoverable. They said, when they saw them expelled out of their own land, "Now <hi type="italic">they shall no more sojourn there;</hi> they have bidden it a final farewell, never more to return to it, for <hi type="italic">God will no more regard them,</hi> and how then can they help themselves?" Herein they were mistaken. God had not cast them off, for all this. Yet thus much is intimated, that all about them observed them to be so very provoking to their God that there was not reason to expect any other than that they should be quite abandoned. <div eID="gen18337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18338" type="x-p"/> III. The despair which they themselves were almost brought to under their calamities. Having heard what they said concerning them <hi type="italic">among the heathen,</hi> let us now hear what they say concerning themselves (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As for us,</hi> we look upon our case to be in a manner helpless. <hi type="italic">Our end is near</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.18">v. 18</reference>), the end both of our church and of our state; we are just at the brink of the ruin of both; nay, <hi type="italic">our end has come;</hi> we are utterly undone; a fatal final period is put to all our comforts; the days of our prosperity are fulfilled; they are numbered and finished." Thus their fears concurred with the hopes of their enemies that the <hi type="italic">Lord would no more regard them.</hi> For, 1. The refuges they fled to disappointed them. They looked for help from this and the other powerful ally, but to no purpose; it proved vain help. The succours they expected did not come in, or at least they had not the success they expected, and their eyes failed with looking for that which never came (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">v. 17</reference>); they <hi type="italic">watched in watching;</hi> they watched long, and with a great deal of earnestness and impatience, <hi type="italic">for a nation</hi> that promised them assistance, but failed them, and frustrated their expectation. They <hi type="italic">could not save them;</hi> they were too weak to contend with the Chaldean army and therefore retired. Help from creatures is vain help (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.11">Ps. lx. 11</reference>), and we may look for it till our eyes fail, till our hearts fail, and come short of it at last. 2. The persecutors they fled from overtook them and overcame them (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">They hunt our steps, that we cannot go in our streets.</hi> When the Chaldeans besieged the city they raised their batteries so high above the walls that they could command the town, and shoot at people as they went along the streets. They <hi type="italic">hunted them</hi> with their arrows from place to place. When the city was broken up, and all the men of war fled, their <hi type="italic">persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven</hi> when they fly upon their prey, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.19">v. 19</reference>. There was no escaping them; they <hi type="italic">pursued them upon the mountains,</hi> and, when they thought they had got clear of them, they fell into the hands of those that <hi type="italic">laid wait for them in the wilderness,</hi> to cut off their retreat, and to pick up stragglers. Nay, the king himself, though he may be supposed to have had all the advantages the exigence of the case would admit to favour his flight, yet could not escape, for divine vengeance pursued him with them, and then (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord, was taken in their pits.</hi> Some apply it to Josiah, who was killed in battle by the king of Egypt; but it is rather to be understood of Zedekiah, who was the last king of the house of David, and who was pursued by the Chaldeans and seized in the plains of Jericho, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jer. xxxix. 5</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">the anointed of the Lord,</hi> heir of that family which God had appointed to the government. He was very much confided in by the Jewish state: <hi type="italic">They said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen.</hi> They promised themselves that the remnant which were left after Jeconiah's captivity should, under the protection of his government, yet again <hi type="italic">take root downward and bear fruit upward.</hi> They thought, though they were so reduced that they could not think of reigning over the heathen, as they had done, yet they might make a shift to live among them and not be insulted and pulled to pieces by them. Thus apt are sinking interests not only to catch at every twig, but to think it will recover them. Jerusalem died of a consumption, a flattering distemper. Even when she was ready to expire she formed some hopeful symptoms to herself, and on them grounded a hope that she should recover; but what came of it? The shadow under which they thought they should live proved like that of Jonah's gourd, which <hi type="italic">withered in a night.</hi> He that was <hi type="italic">the anointed of the Lord was taken in their pits,</hi> as if he had been but a beast of prey; so little account did they make of a person deemed sacred and not to be violated. Note, When we make any creature <hi type="italic">the breath of our nostrils,</hi> and promise ourselves that we shall live by it, it is just with God to stop that breath, and deprive us of the life we expected by it; for God will have the honour of being himself along <hi type="italic">our life and the length of our days.</hi>
entries.817f32b4a8b8aa8514298997208e593b53b4268b: <div eID="gen18338" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Comfort for Zion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18339" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz; the cup also shall pass through unto thee: thou shalt be drunken, and shalt make thyself naked. <hi type="super">22</hi> The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion; he will no more carry thee away into captivity: he will visit thine iniquity, O daughter of Edom; he will discover thy sins. <div eID="gen18339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18340" type="x-p"/> David's psalms of lamentation commonly conclude with some word of comfort, which is as life from the dead and light shining out of darkness; so does this lamentation here in this chapter. The people of God are now in great distress, their aspects all doleful, their prospects all frightful, and their ill-natured neighbours the Edomites insult over them and do all they can to exasperate their destroyers against them. Such was their violence against their brother Jacob (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.10">Obad. 10</reference>), such their spleen at Jerusalem, of which they cried, <hi type="italic">Rase it, rase it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Ps. cxxxvii. 7</reference>. Now it is here foretold, for the encouragement of God's people, <div eID="gen18340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18341" type="x-p"/> I. That an end shall be put to Zion's troubles (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">The punishment of they iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion!</hi> not the fulness of that punishment which it deserves, but of that which God has designed and determined to inflict, and which was necessary to answer the end, the glorifying of God's justice and the taking away of their sin. The captivity, which is <hi type="italic">the punishment of thy iniquity, is accomplished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa. xl. 2</reference>), and <hi type="italic">he will no longer keep thee in captivity;</hi> so it may be read, as well as, <hi type="italic">he will no more carry thee into captivity;</hi> he will turn again thy captivity and work a glorious release for thee. Note, The troubles of God's people shall be continued no longer than till they have done their work for which they were sent. <div eID="gen18341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18342" type="x-p"/> II. That an end shall be put to Edom's triumphs. It is spoken ironically (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom!</hi> go on to insult over Zion in distress, till thou hast filled up the measure of thy iniquity. Do so; rejoice in thy own present exemption from the common fate of thy neighbours." This is like Solomon's upbraiding the young man with his ungoverned mirth (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Rejoice, O young man! in thy youth;</hi> rejoice, if thou canst, when God comes to reckon with thee, and that he will do ere long. <hi type="italic">The cup</hi> of trembling, which it is now Jerusalem's turn to drink deeply of, <hi type="italic">shall pass through unto thee;</hi> it shall go round till it comes to be thy lot to pledge it." Note, This is a good reason why we should not insult over any who are in misery, because we ourselves also are in the body, and we know not how soon their case may be ours. But those who please themselves in the calamities of God's church must expect to have their doom, as aiders and abettors, with those that are instrumental in those calamities. The destruction of the Edomites was foretold by this prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer. xlix. 7</reference>. &c.), and the people of God must encourage themselves against their present rudeness and insolence with the prospect of it. 1. It will be a shameful destruction: "<hi type="italic">The cup</hi> that <hi type="italic">shall pass unto thee</hi> shall intoxicate thee" (and that is shame enough to any man); "<hi type="italic">thou shalt be drunken,</hi> quite infatuated, and at thy wits' end, shalt stagger in all thy counsels and stumble in all thy enterprises, and then, as Noah when he was drunk, <hi type="italic">thou shalt make thyself naked</hi> and expose thyself to contempt." Note, Those who ridicule God's people will justly be left to themselves to do that, some time or other, by which they will be made ridiculous. 2. It will be a righteous destruction. God will herein <hi type="italic">visit thy iniquity</hi> and <hi type="italic">discover thy sins;</hi> he will punish them, and, to justify himself therein, he will discover them, and make it to appear that he has just cause thus to proceed against them. Nay, the punishment of the sin shall so exactly answer the sin that it shall itself plainly discover it. Sometimes God does so visit the iniquity that he that runs may read the sin in the punishment. But, sooner or later, sin will be visited and discovered, and all the hidden works of darkness brought to light.  <chapter eID="Lam.4"/> <div eID="gen18342" type="x-p"/>

Sodom--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.11.23">Mt 11:23</reference>). entries.1828d9a2402915884eea9b33b34f7a2492dc43c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10905"/><div sID="gen19616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10905"/><hi type="bold">7. (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.8-Dan.1.15">Da 1:8-15</reference>). Also David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.12">1Sa 16:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.42">17:42</reference>). Type of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen19616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rubies--</hi>Gesenius translates, "corals," from a Hebrew root, "to divide into branches," from the branching form of corals.<div eID="gen19617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">polishing--</hi>They were like exquisitely cut and polished sapphires. entries.5a11822d14a60faa792dc8f560e594c647642201: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10909"/><div sID="gen19631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10909"/><hi type="bold">11. fire ... devoured ... foundations--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.22">De 32:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.14">Jr 21:14</reference>). A most rare event. Fire usually consumes only the surface; but this reached even to the foundation, cutting off all hope of restoration.<div eID="gen19631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19632" type="x-p"/> Lamed. <div eID="gen19632" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ecf19e16f7e84a0e5266ba18ad0e108d6a1cee4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10910"/><div sID="gen19633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10910"/>12. Jerusalem was so fortified that all thought it impregnable. It therefore could only have been the hand of God, not the force of man, which overthrew it.<div eID="gen19633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19634" type="x-p"/> Mem. <div eID="gen19634" type="x-p"/>
entries.482eb83861cd50635b96ccadd3c0e5646e9ba6ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10911"/><div sID="gen19635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10911"/><hi type="bold">13. prophets--</hi>the false prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.11">Jr 23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">21</reference>). Supply the sense thus: "For the sins ... these calamities have befallen her."<div eID="gen19635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shed the blood of the just--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.23.31">Mt 23:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">37</reference>). This received its full fulfilment in the slaying of Messiah and the Jews' consequent dispersion (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.6">Jas 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19637" type="x-p"/> Nun. <div eID="gen19637" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d5645ace1218aafe40ed8a23a94555bed1b5869: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10912"/><div sID="gen19638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10912"/><hi type="bold">14. blind--</hi>with mental aberration.<div eID="gen19638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">polluted ... with blood--</hi>both with blood of one another mutually shed (for example, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.34">Jr 2:34</reference>), and with their blood shed by the enemy [Glassius].<div eID="gen19639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not touch ... garments--</hi>as being defiled with blood (<reference osisRef="Num.19.16">Nu 19:16</reference>).<div eID="gen19640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19641" type="x-p"/> Samech. <div eID="gen19641" type="x-p"/>
entries.454e0cf5637783844c7ff584c852aef5af7a7404: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10913"/><div sID="gen19642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10913"/><hi type="bold">15. They ... them--</hi>"They," that is, "men" (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.14">La 4:14</reference>). Even the very Gentiles, regarded as unclean by the Jews, who were ordered most religiously to avoid all defilements, cried unto the latter, "depart," as being unclean: so universal was the defilement of the city by blood.<div eID="gen19642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wandered--</hi>As the false prophets and their followers had "wandered" blind with infatuated and idolatrous crime in the city (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.14">La 4:14</reference>), so they must now "wander" among the heathen in blind consternation with calamity.<div eID="gen19643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they said--</hi>that is, the Gentiles said: it was said among the heathen, "The Jews shall no more sojourn in their own land" [Grotius]; or, wheresoever they go in their wandering exile, "they shall not stay long" [Ludovicus De Dieu], (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.65">De 28:65</reference>).<div eID="gen19644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19645" type="x-p"/> Pe. <div eID="gen19645" type="x-p"/>
entries.4765476970e97b40141c595941b6260f39f59495: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10914"/><div sID="gen19646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10914"/>16. Ain and Pe are here transposed (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">La 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">17</reference>), as in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">La 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>; 3:46-51.<div eID="gen19646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anger--</hi>literally, "face"; it is the countenance which, by its expression, manifests anger (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">Psa 34:16</reference>). Gesenius translates, "the person of Jehovah"; Jehovah present; Jehovah Himself (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.14">Ex 33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.11">2Sa 17:11</reference>).<div eID="gen19647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19648" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divided--</hi>dispersed the Jews.<div eID="gen19648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they respected not ... priests--</hi>This is the language of the Gentiles. "The Jews have no hope of a return: for they respected not even good priests" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.19-2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:19-22</reference>) [Grotius]. Maurer explains it, "They (the victorious foe) regard not the (Jewish) priests when imploring their pity" (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">La 5:12</reference>). The evident antithesis to "As for us" (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">La 4:17</reference>) and the language of "the heathen" at the close of <reference osisRef="Lam.4.15">La 4:15</reference>, of which <reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">La 4:16</reference> is the continuation, favor the former view.<div eID="gen19649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19650" type="x-p"/> Ain. <div eID="gen19650" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa970e4613f2be2df0061688f661584731ca4eba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10915"/><div sID="gen19651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10915"/><hi type="bold">17. As for us--</hi>This translation forms the best antithesis to the language of the heathen (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.15">La 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">16</reference>). Calvin translates, "While as yet we stood as a state, our eyes failed," &c.<div eID="gen19651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watched for a nation that could not save us--</hi>Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Is 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5-Jer.37.11">Jr 37:5-11</reference>).<div eID="gen19652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19653" type="x-p"/> Tzaddi. <div eID="gen19653" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f20cd3dc7a56ab03bb9c0318ce4c409432d5d78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10916"/><div sID="gen19654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10916"/><hi type="bold">18. They--</hi>the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen19654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot go--</hi>without danger.<div eID="gen19655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19656" type="x-p"/> Koph. <div eID="gen19656" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d520b980bfa2888e55500f8dfe8a6f8ce9858d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10917"/><div sID="gen19657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10917"/>19. The last times just before the taking of the city. There was no place of escape; the foe intercepted those wishing to escape from the famine-stricken city, "on the mountains and in the wilderness."<div eID="gen19657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swifter ... than ... eagles--</hi>the Chaldean cavalry (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jr 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen19658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pursued--</hi>literally, "to be hot"; then, "to pursue hotly" (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.36">Ge 31:36</reference>). Thus they pursued and overtook Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.8">Jr 52:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen19659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19660" type="x-p"/> Resh. <div eID="gen19660" type="x-p"/>
entries.0780a7fc230f3a55760f0051a49ae5af34e2ab4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10918"/><div sID="gen19661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10918"/><hi type="bold">20. breath ... anointed of ... Lord--</hi>our king, with whose life ours was bound up. The original reference seems to have been to Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2Ch 35:25</reference>), killed in battle with Pharaoh-necho; but the language is here applied to Zedekiah, who, though worthless, was still lineal representative of David, and type of Messiah, the "Anointed." Viewed personally the language is too favorable to apply to him.<div eID="gen19661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live among the heathen--</hi>Under him we hoped to live securely, even in spite of the surrounding heathen nations [Grotius].<div eID="gen19662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19663" type="x-p"/> Schin. <div eID="gen19663" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b10605d9abf4571ba2809110ab369ef890717a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10919"/><div sID="gen19664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10919"/><hi type="bold">21. Rejoice--</hi>at our calamities (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>). This is a prophecy that Edom should exult over the fall of Jerusalem. At the same time it is implied, Edom's joy shall be short-lived. Ironically she is told, Rejoice while thou mayest (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>).<div eID="gen19664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cup--</hi>for this image of the confounding effects of God's wrath, see <reference osisRef="Jer.13.12">Jr 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">25:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.21">16, 21</reference>; as to Edom, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7-Jer.49.22">Jr 49:7-22</reference>.<div eID="gen19665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19666" type="x-p"/> Tau. <div eID="gen19666" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf54c0bb76f2d0ad13a6e53111e12a3dbfc6d2bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10920"/><div sID="gen19667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10920"/>22. (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Is 40:2</reference>). Thou hast been punished enough: the end of thy punishment is at hand.<div eID="gen19667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no more carry thee ... into captivity--</hi>that is, by the Chaldeans. The Romans carried them away subsequently. The full accomplishment of this prophecy must therefore refer to the Jews' final restoration.<div eID="gen19668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">discover--</hi>By the severity of His punishments on thee, God shall let men see how great was thy sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.10">Jr 49:10</reference>). God "covers" sin when He forgives it (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">5</reference>). He "discovers," or "reveals," it, when He punishes it (<reference osisRef="Job.20.27">Job 20:27</reference>). <reference osisRef="Jer.49.10">Jr 49:10</reference> shows that Margin is wrong, "carry captive" (this rendering is as in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.7">Na 2:7</reference>; compare "discovered," Margin). <chapter eID="Lam.4"/>

entries.a05c6efa682834208a9c434144e4710f30522d95: <div eID="gen31068" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31069" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31070" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31070" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31069" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31071" type="x-p"/> The present deplorable sate of the nation is now contrasted with its ancient prosperity, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.12">Lam 4:1-12</reference>; and the unhappy change ascribed, in a great degree, to the profligacy of the priests and prophets, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.13-Lam.4.16">Lam 4:13-16</reference>. The national calamities are tenderly lamented, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.17-Lam.4.20">Lam 4:17-20</reference>. The ruin of the Edomites also, who had insulted the Jews in their distress, is ironically predicted, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">Lam 4:21</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Psa.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Oba.1.10-Oba.1.12">Oba 1:10-12</reference>. The chapter closes with a gracious promise of deliverance from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">Lam 4:22</reference>. <div eID="gen31071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31072" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31073" type="x-p"/> How is the gold become dim - The prophet contrasts, in various affecting instances, the wretched circumstances of the Jewish nation, with the flourishing state of their affairs in former times. Here they are compared to gold, זהב zahab, native gold from the mine, which, contrary to its nature, is become dim, is tarnished; and even the fine, the sterling gold, כתם kethem, that which was stamped to make it current, is changed or adulterated, so as to be no longer passable. This might be applied to the temple, but particularly to the fallen priests and apostate prophets. <div eID="gen31073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31074" type="x-p"/> The stones of the sanctuary - אבני קדש abney kodesh, the holy stones; the Jewish godly men, who were even then the living stones of which God built his Church.
entries.ad34da429254a65bb7929fd9193858a8e2822908: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31075" type="x-p"/> The precious sons of Zion - The Jewish priests and Jewish believers. <div eID="gen31075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31076" type="x-p"/> Comparable to fine gold - Who were of the pure standard of holiness; holy, because God who called them is holy; but now esteemed no better than earthen pitchers - vessels of dishonor in comparison of what they once were.
entries.1069b3265bf37bb37144b2592e18541c7422ae0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31077" type="x-p"/> Even the sea monsters draw out the breast - The whales give suck to their young ones. The word תנין tannin, signifies all large and cruel creatures, whether aquatic or terrestrial; and need not here be restrained to the former sort. My Old MS. Bible translates curiously: Not and the cruel bestis that ben clepid Lamya, and thei nakeden ther tetis, geve ther whelpis souken. <div eID="gen31077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31078" type="x-p"/> Like the ostriches in the wilderness - For her carelessness about her eggs, and her inattention to her young, the ostrich is proverbial.
entries.3be63a792f193fc2ea03e9d58feaa075ea90ebfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31079" type="x-p"/> The tongue of the sucking child - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lam.2.12">Lam 2:12</reference> (note).
entries.7beda61adeaae219248326a7d21f3f918f1a09bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31080" type="x-p"/> Embrace dunghills - Lie on straw or rubbish, instead of the costly carpets and sofas on which they formerly stretched themselves.
entries.b0ff9ff84faf67cf0a9eb881d42ad564ffbedde6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31081" type="x-p"/> For the punishment - He thinks the punishment of Jerusalem far greater than that of Sodom. That was destroyed in a moment while all her inhabitants were in health and strength; Jerusalem fell by the most lingering calamities; her men partly destroyed by the sword, and partly by the famine. <div eID="gen31081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31082" type="x-p"/> Instead of no hands stayed on her, Blayney translates, "Nor were hands weakened in her." Perhaps the meaning is, "Sodom was destroyed in a moment without any human labor." It was a judgment from God himself: so the sacred text: "The Lord rained down fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven." See <reference osisRef="Gen.19.24">Gen 19:24</reference>.
entries.ee2231301f4b4d4496595d322a2e5b7d08ace3b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31083" type="x-p"/> Her Nazarites were purer than snow - נזיר nazir does not always signify a person separated under a religious vow; it sometimes denotes what is chief or eminent. It is applied to Joseph, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.26">Gen 49:26</reference>. <div eID="gen31083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31084" type="x-p"/> Blayney therefore translates here, Her Nobles. "Her nobles were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk; <div eID="gen31084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31085" type="x-p"/> They were ruddier on the bone than rubies; their veining was the sapphires." <div eID="gen31085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31086" type="x-p"/> On which he remarks: - "In the first line the whiteness of their skin is described, and in the second, their flesh;" and as גזר gazar signifies to divide and intersect, as the blue veins do on the surface of the body, these are without doubt intended. <div eID="gen31086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31087" type="x-p"/> Milk will most certainly well apply to the whiteness of the skin; the beautiful ruby to the ruddiness of the flesh; and the sapphire, in its clear transcendent purple, to the veins in a fine complexion. The reverse of this state, as described in the following verse, needs no explanation. The face was a dismal dark brown, the flesh gone, the skin shrivelled, and apparently wrapped round the bones.
entries.a7cd2d35065aa4978938255f0e95d791941031f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31088" type="x-p"/> The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children - See on <reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">Lam 2:20</reference> (note). But here there is a reference to mothers eating their own children; and this was done, not by mothers cruel and brutal, but by נשים רחמניות nashim rachmaniyoth, the compassionate, the tender-hearted mothers. From these horrible scenes it is well to pass with as hasty a step as possible.
entries.adb014f1352bad319818a8d09078152710a98f9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31089" type="x-p"/> The kings of the earth - Jerusalem was so well fortified, both by nature and art, that it appeared as a miracle that it should be taken at all.
entries.366b4e155daf45023651e00331bf1f17e79dc791: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31090" type="x-p"/> For the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests - These most wretched beings, under the pretense of zeal for the true religion, persecuted the genuine prophets, priests, and people of God, and caused their blood to be shed in the midst of the city, in the most open and public manner; exactly as the murderous priests, and blood-thirsty preachers, under the reign of bloody Queen Mary, did in England. However, the profligate priests and idolatrous prophets in Jerusalem, only shed the blood of the saints of God there: but the sanguinary papists, in the above reign, burnt the blood here, for they burnt the people alive; and at the same time, in their worse than Molochean cruelty, consigned, with all the fervor peculiar to their then ruthless Church, the souls of those whom they thus massacred, to the bitter pains of eternal death! O earth, cover not thou their blood!
entries.65793f5ff2fbe297b5048079da5fd490671b8a6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31091" type="x-p"/> They have wandered as blind men in the streets - Rather, "They ran frantic through the streets, they were stained with blood." This was in their pretended zeal for their cause. Bishop Bonner, who was at the head of those sanguinary executions in England, was accustomed to buffet the poor Protestants, when on their examinations they were too powerful for him in argument: - "He proved his doctrine orthodox, <div eID="gen31091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31092" type="x-p"/> By apostolic blows and knocks." <div eID="gen31092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31093" type="x-p"/> Just as his elder brethren, the false priests and prophets of Jerusalem.
entries.b95afba4539072156c5a1318e7695d12414ce5b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen31093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31094" type="x-p"/> When they fled away - These priests and prophets were so bad, that the very heathen did not like to permit them to sojourn among them. The prophet now resumes the history of the siege.
entries.f0391094f98abf1c9ebdc98aea4483473b618c3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31095" type="x-p"/> We have watched for a nation - Viz., the Egyptians, who were their pretended allies, but were neither able nor wilting to help them against the Chaldeans.
entries.b2c1e7696ed2dbf6776b03c834fc4f23aa5e485a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31096" type="x-p"/> We cannot go in our streets - Supposed to refer to the darts and other missiles cast from the mounds which they had raised on the outside of the walls, by which those who walked in the streets were grievously annoyed, and could not shield themselves.
entries.aec58697c5823eb91ea53249ded35707443d413f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen31096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31097" type="x-p"/> They pursued us upon the mountains - They hunted down the poor Jews like wild beasts in every part of the country by their marauding parties, whilst the great army besieged Jerusalem. But this may apply to the pursuit of Zedekiah. See what follows.
entries.6c4616ba307583b592e4e76a09c08409468295a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen31097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31098" type="x-p"/> The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord - That is, Zedekiah the king, who was as the life or the city, was taken in his flight by the Chaldeans, and his eyes were put out; so that he was wholly unfit to perform any function of government; though they had fondly hoped that if they surrendered and should be led captives, yet they should be permitted to live under their own laws and king in the land of their bondage.
entries.814196037f8a895235b8f30c0c086e2198bb8d29: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen31098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31099" type="x-p"/> Rejoice and be Lad, O daughter of Edom - A strong irony. <div eID="gen31099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31100" type="x-p"/> The cup also shall pass through unto thee - Thou who hast triumphed in our disasters shalt shortly have enough of thy own. They had joined themselves to the Chaldeans, (see <reference osisRef="Psa.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>), and therefore they should share in the desolations of Babylon.
entries.33e3e0b62a83f236f983121d51917a486338bf6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31101" type="x-p"/> The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion - On the contrary: Rejoice, O Jerusalem, for thy captivity will soon end; thy sufferings are nearly completed; thou shalt soon return to thy own land: but he will visit thy iniquity, O Edom; he will discover thy sins. When sin is pardoned it is said to be covered: here, God says he will not cover the sins of Edom - he will not pardon them; they shall drink the cup of wrath. <div eID="gen31101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31102" type="x-p"/> The promise in this last verse may refer to Jerusalem under the Gospel. When they receive Christ crucified, they shall be gathered from all nations, become one with the Church among the Gentiles, be one flock under one and the same Shepherd, and shall be carried no more into captivity.  <chapter eID="Lam.4"/> <div eID="gen31102" type="x-p"/>

entries.52a166ab7b66cac6485619e4cb0d4bd7e75697d0: <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.22">Lamentations 4:1-22</reference> <div eID="gen14721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14722" type="x-p"/> The lamentation over the terrible calamity that has befallen Jerusalem is distinguished in this poem from the lamentations in Lamentations 1 and 2, not merely by the fact that in it the fate of the several classes of the population is contemplated, but chiefly by the circumstance that the calamity is set forth as a well-merited punishment by God for the grievous sins of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. This consideration forms the chief feature in the whole poem, from the beginning to the end of which there predominates the hope that Zion will not perish, but that the appointed punishment will terminate, and then fall on their now triumphant enemies. In this fundamental idea of the poem, compared with the first two, there is plainly an advance towards the due recognition of the suffering as a punishment; from this point it is possible to advance, not merely to the hope regarding the future, with which the poem concludes, but also the prayer for deliverance in Lamentations 5. The contents of the poem are the following: The princes and inhabitants of Zion are sunk into a terrible state of misery, because their guilt was greater than the sin of Sodom (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.11">Lam 4:1-11</reference>). Jerusalem has been delivered into the hands of her enemies on account of her prophets and priests, who have shed the blood of righteous ones (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.12-Lam.4.16">Lam 4:12-16</reference>), and because the people have placed their trust on the vain help of man (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.17-Lam.4.20">Lam 4:17-20</reference>). For this they must atone; for the present, however, the enemy may triumph; the guilt of the daughter of Zion will come to an end, and then the judgment will befall her enemies (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">Lam 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">Lam 4:22</reference>). <div eID="gen14722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14723" type="x-p"/> The misery that has come on the inhabitants of Jerusalem is a punishment for their deep guilt. The description given of this misery is divided into two strophes: for, first (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.6">Lam 4:1-6</reference>), the sad lot of the several classes of the population is set forth; then (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.7-Lam.4.11">Lam 4:7-11</reference>) a conclusion is drawn therefrom regarding the greatness of their sin. <div eID="gen14723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14724" type="x-p"/> The first strophe. Lam 4:1. The lamentation begins with a figurative account of the destruction of all that is precious and glorious in Israel: this is next established by the bringing forth of instances. <div eID="gen14724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14725" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.2">Lam 4:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen14725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14726" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">Lam 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">Lam 4:2</reference> contain, not a complaint regarding the desolation of the sanctuary and of Zion, as Maurer, Kalkschmidt, and Thenius, with the lxx, assume, but, as is unmistakeably declared in <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">Lam 4:2</reference>, a lamentation over the fearful change that has taken place in the fate of the citizens of Zion. What is stated in <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">Lam 4:1</reference> regarding the gold and the precious stones must be understood figuratively; and in the case of the "gold that has become dim," we can as little think of the blackening of the gilding in the temple fabric when it was burnt, as think of bricks (Thenius) when "the holy stones" are spoken of. The בּני ציּון (inhabitants of Zion), <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">Lam 4:2</reference>, are likened to gold and sacred stones; here Thenius would arbitrarily change בּני into בּתּי (houses, palaces). This change not merely has no critical support, but is objectionable on the simple ground that there is not a single word to be found elsewhere, through all the chapter, concerning the destruction of the temple and the palaces; it is merely the fate of the men, not of the buildings, that is bewailed. "How is gold bedimmed!" יוּעם is the Hophal of עמם, to be dark, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.3">Eze 28:3</reference>, and to darken, Eze 31:8. The second clause, "how is fine gold changed!" expresses the same thing. שׁנא = שׁנה, according to the Chaldaizing usage, means to change (oneself), Mal 3:6. The growing dim and the changing refer to the colour, the loss of brilliancy; for gold does not alter in substance. B. C. Michaelis and Rosenmüller are too specific when they explain that the gold represents <hi type="italic">populus Judaicus (</hi>or the<hi type="italic">potior populi Hebraei pars), qui (quae) quondam auri instar in sanctuario Dei fulgebat</hi>, and when they see in אבּני קדשׁ an allusion to the stones in the breast-plate of the high priest. Gold is generally an emblem of very worthy persons, and "holy stones" are precious stones, intended for a sacred purpose. Both expressions collectively form a figurative description of the people of Israel, as called to be a holy nation and a kingdom of priests. Analogous is the designation of the children of Israel as אבּני נזר, Zec 9:16 (Gerlach). השׁתּפּך, to be poured out (at all the corners of the streets), is a figurative expression, signifying disgraceful treatment, as in Lam 2:11. In <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">Lam 4:2</reference> follows the application of the figure to the sons (i.e., the citizens) of Zion, not merely the chief nobles of Judah (Ewald), or the princes, nor children in the narrowest sense of the word (Gerlach); for in what follows mention is made not only of children (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.3">Lam 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.4">Lam 4:4</reference>), but also of those who are grown up (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.5">Lam 4:5</reference>), and princes are not mentioned till Lam 4:7. As being members of the chosen people, all the inhabitants of Jerusalem have been held "dear," and "weighed out with gold," i.e., esteemed as of equal value with gold (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.19">Job 28:19</reference>); but now, when Jerusalem is destroyed, they have become regarded as earthenware pots, i.e., treated as if they were utterly worthless, as "a work of the hands of the potter," whereas Israel was a work of the hands of God, Isa 64:7. סלא = סלה, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.19">Job 28:19</reference> to weigh; Pual, be weighed out, as an equivalent.
entries.1d3b7127a18f518594d4169210c455d56cd56b48: <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3">Lam 4:3</reference> <div eID="gen14726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14727" type="x-p"/> This disregard or rejection of the citizens of Zion is evidence in <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3">Lam 4:3</reference> and onwards by many examples, beginning with children, ascending to adults (3-5), and ending with princes. The starvation to death of the children (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.3">Lam 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.4">Lam 4:4</reference>) is mentioned first; and the frightful misery that has befallen Jerusalem is vividly set forth, by a comparison of the way in which wild animals act towards their young with the behaviour of the mothers of Jerusalem towards their children. Even jackals (תּנּין for תּנּים, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">Jer 9:10</reference>) give their breasts to their young ones to suck. חלצוּ , <hi type="italic">extrahunt mammam</hi> = they present their breast. As Junius has remarked, the expression is taken a <hi type="italic">mulieribus lactantibus, quae laxata veste mammam lactanti praebent</hi>; hence also we are not, for the sake of this expression, to understand תּנּין as meaning <hi type="italic">cetus</hi> (Bochart and Nägelsbach), regarding which animal Bochart remarks (<hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. iii. p. 777, ed. Rosenmüller), <hi type="italic">ceti papillas non esse</hi>ἐπιφανεῖς, <hi type="italic">quippe in mammis receptae tanquam in vaginis conduntur</hi>. Rosenmüller has already rejected this meaning as <hi type="italic">minus apta</hi> for the present passage. From the combination of jackals and ostriches as inhabiting desert places (Isa 13:21.; <reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>), we have no hesitation in fixing on "jackals" as the meaning here. "The daughter of my people" (cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">Lam 2:11</reference>) here means the inhabitants of Zion or Jerusalem. לאכזר, "has become cruel." The <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> כי ענים instead of כּיענים (<hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>) may possibly have arisen from a purely accidental separation of the letters of the word in a MS, a reading which was afterwards painfully retained by the scribes. But in many codices noted by Kennicott and De Rossi, as well as in several old editions, the word is found correctly joined, without any marginal note. יענים means ostriches, usually בּת יענה ("daughter of crying," or according to Gesenius, in his <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>, and Ewald, following the Syriac, "the daughter of gluttony"), the female ostrich. The comparison with these animals is to be understood in accordance with <reference osisRef="Job.39.16">Job 39:16</reference> : "she (the female ostrich) treats her young ones harshly, as if they were not her own." This popular belief is founded on the fact that the animal lays her eggs in the ground, - after having done no more than slightly scratching up the soil, - and partly also, when the nest is full, on the surface of the ground; she then leaves them to be hatched, in course of time, by the heat of the sun: the eggs may thus be easily broken, see on <reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference>-16.
entries.9438feb0aeee80995981557d6344e0caf42742ff: <reference osisRef="Lam.4.4-Lam.4.5">Lam 4:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen14727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14728" type="x-p"/> Sucking infants and little children perish from thirst and hunger; cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">Lam 2:11</reference>-12. פּרשׂ = פּרס, as in Mic 3:3, to break down into pieces, break bread = divide, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa 58:7</reference>; Jer 16:7. In <reference osisRef="Lam.4.5">Lam 4:5</reference> it is not children, but adults, that are spoken of. למעדנּים is variously rendered, since אכל occurs nowhere else in construction with ל. Against the assumption that ל is the Aramaic sign of the object, there stands the fact that אכל is not found thus construed with ל, either in the Lamentations or elsewhere, though in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.2">Jer 40:2</reference> ל is so used. Gerlach, accordingly, would take למעדנּים adverbially, as meaning "after their heart’s desire," prop. for pleasures (as to this meaning, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.17">Pro 29:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32">1Sa 15:32</reference>), in contrast with אכל לשׂבע, to eat for satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.3">Exo 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.19">Lev 25:19</reference>, etc. But "for pleasure" is not an appropriate antithesis to satisfaction. Hence we prefer, with Thenius, to take אכל ל in the sense of nibbling round something, in which there is contained the notion of selection in the eating; we also take מעדנּים, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.20">Gen 49:20</reference>, to mean dainties. נשׁמּוּ, to be made desolate, as in <reference osisRef="Lam.1.13">Lam 1:13</reference>, of the destruction of happiness in life; with בּחוּצות, to sit in a troubled or gloomy state of mind on the streets. האמנים, those who (as children) were carried on purple (תּולע for שׁני rof תּו towla`at תּולעת, cochineal, crimson), embrace (i.e., cling to) dung-heaps, seek them as places or rest.
entries.db29fe13b54596fb9d32f671b1553547b32e161a: <reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">Lam 4:6</reference> <div eID="gen14728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14729" type="x-p"/> The greatness of their guilt is seen in this misery. The ו consecutive joined with יגדּל here marks the result, so far as this manifests itself: "thus the offence (guilt) of the daughter of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom." Most expositors take עון and הטּאת dna  here in the sense of punishment; but this meaning has not been established. The words simply mean "offence" and "sin," sometimes including their consequences, but nowhere do they mean unceremonious castigation. But when Thenius is of opinion that the context demands the meaning "punishment" (not "sin"), he has inconsiderately omitted the ו <hi type="italic">consec</hi>., and taken a wrong view of the context. הפך is the usual word employed in connection with the destruction of Sodom; cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.19.21">Gen 19:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.25">Gen 19:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>, etc. 'ולא חלוּ וגו is translated by Thenius, <hi type="italic">et non torquebatur in ea manus</hi>, i.e., without any one wringing his hands. However, חוּל (to go in a circle) means to writhe with pain, but does not agree with ידים, to wring the hands. In Hos 11:6 חוּל is used of the sword, which "circles" in the cities, i.e., cuts and kills all round in them. In like manner it is here used of the hands that went round in Sodom for the purpose of overthrowing (destroying) the city. Nägelsbach wrongly derives חלוּ from חלה, to become slack, powerless. The words, "no hands went round (were at work) in her," serve to explain the meaning of כּמו רגע, "as in a moment," without any need for the hands of men being engaged in it. By this additional remark, not merely is greater prominence given to the sudden destruction of Sodom by the hand of God; but it is also pointed out how far Jerusalem, in comparison with that judgment of God, suffers a greater punishment for her greater sins: for her destruction by the hand of man brings her more enduring torments. "Sodom’s suffering at death was brief; for there were no children dying of hunger, no mothers who boiled their children" (Nägelsbach). Sodom was spared this heartrending misery, inasmuch as it was destroyed by the hand of God in an instant.
entries.bdae665aafe05cc920cea3825e244fed80ad50f8: <reference osisRef="Lam.4.7-Lam.4.8">Lam 4:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen14729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14730" type="x-p"/> The second strophe. - <reference osisRef="Lam.4.7">Lam 4:7</reference>, Lam 4:8. The picture of the misery that has befallen the princes. נזירים, princes, prop. <hi type="italic">separati</hi>, here <hi type="italic">non voto</hi> (Nazarites<hi type="italic">) sed dignitate</hi>, as Nolde appropriately remarks; see on Gen 49:26. זכך is used, <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">Job 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">Job 25:5</reference>, of the brightness of the heaven and the stars; here it is used of female beauty. Thenius would refer "pure (or bright) as snow and milk" to the white clothing, "because the Orientals have not milk-white faces." But the second member irrefragably shows that the reference is to bodily form; and for the very reason adduced by Thenius, a comparatively whiter skin than is commonly met with is esteemed more beautiful. So also does Sol 5:10, "My friend is white and red," show the high esteem in which beauty was held (Gerlach). אדם, to be reddish. עצם, "bone," for the body (<hi type="italic">pars pro toto</hi>). פּנינים, not (white) pearls, but (red) corals. "The white and the red are to be understood as mixed, and shading into one another, as our popular poetry speaks of cheeks which 'like milk and purple shine' " (Delitzsch on <reference osisRef="Job.28.18">Job 28:18</reference>, Clark’s translation). "Sapphire their form" (גּזרה, prop. cut, <hi type="italic">taille</hi>, of the shape of the body). The point of the comparison is not the colour, but the luminosity, of this precious stone. Once on a time the princes glittered so; but (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.8">Lam 4:8</reference>) now their form is dark as blackness, i.e., every trace of beauty and splendour has vanished.
